eng-u2-cloze2.title: Bài đọc đục lỗ Unit 2 (band 7.0–8.5) — A bowl of heritage
eng-u2-cloze2.text: Pho, Vietnam's most celebrated dish, (1) ____ humble origins in the early twentieth century. eng-u1-cloze4.title: Bài đọc đục lỗ Unit 1 (nâng cao) — Beyond recognition
eng-u1-cloze4.text: Marie Curie remains the only person to have won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences. After Pierre (4) ____ in a street accident in 1906, she succeeded him at the Sorbonne. (5) ____ chronic illness caused by prolonged exposure to radiation, she drove mobile X-ray units to the front lines during World War I. Her laboratory notebooks, still too radioactive to handle safely, remind us (6) ____ her sacrifice.

eng-u2-cloze4.title: Bài đọc đục lỗ Unit 2 (nâng cao) — Living together, apart?

eng-u1-rc1.title: Bài đọc hiểu Unit 1 (nâng cao) — The Lady with the Lamp
eng-u1-rc1.text: Florence Nightingale is remembered as the founder of modern nursing, yet her real achievement was less romantic than the legend of the Lady with the Lamp suggests. Born into a wealthy British family, she defied her parents by training as a nurse — then considered menial work unsuitable for a lady. During the Crimean War, she led a team of nurses to a military hospital where soldiers were dying more from infections than from wounds. By enforcing basic hygiene — clean bandages, ventilation, and proper nutrition — she drastically reduced the death rate. Her polar-area diagrams, an early form of infographics, persuaded a skeptical government that sanitation saved lives. After the war, she used her fame to establish the first professional nursing school in London. Bedridden for much of her later life, she continued to advise on hospital reform through voluminous correspondence. Nightingale's story illustrates how perseverance coupled with evidence can overturn entrenched practices.

eng-u1-cloze5.title: Bài đọc đục lỗ Unit 1 (nâng cao) — The making of a legend

While archives (3) ____ a more complex picture, the public often prefers a flawless hero. By 2010, scholars (4) ____ most of these myths, yet revised editions rarely attract the same enthusiasm. (5) ____ the demand for role models, publishers continue to favour hagiography over complexity. A mature reader, therefore, treats every life story not as gospel as a source of (6) ____.

eng-u1-450-rc1.title: Bài đọc hiểu Unit 1 Code 450 – The unbelievable life of Malala Yousafzai
eng-u1-450-rc1.text:
Malala Yousafzai's life story is one of incredible courage and resilience, and it continues to inspire millions around the world. Born in 1997 in the Swat Valley of Pakistan, a region where the Taliban's control over education meant girls were often denied the right to go to school, Malala's path to becoming an international icon for girls' education began at an early age.

From a young age, Malala was determined to get an education. Her father, Ziauddin Yousafzai, was an outspoken educator and activist, and he encouraged her to speak out about the importance of education, especially for girls. When Malala was just 11 years old, she began writing a blog for the BBC Urdu under a pseudonym, detailing her life under Taliban rule and her dreams of going to school. She quickly became a powerful voice for girls in Pakistan who were deprived of education.

However, Malala's activism put her in the crosshairs of the Taliban. On October 9, 2012, when she was just 15 years old, a Taliban gunman boarded her school bus, shot her in the head, and left her for dead. The world was stunned by the attack, and many feared Malala would not survive. But against all odds, Malala not only survived but continued her mission. She was flown to the UK for treatment and rehabilitation, and the attack only made her more determined to fight for girls' education worldwide.

Malala's recovery was nothing short of miraculous, and she soon became a global symbol of resistance to oppression. She continued her advocacy on the world stage, speaking at the United Nations and becoming the youngest-ever recipient of the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014 at the age of 17. Through her work with the Malala Fund, Malala has been advocating for girls' education and empowerment around the world, particularly in areas affected by conflict.

Malala's life journey is a testament to the power of education and the strength of one voice to change the world. From a young girl who was almost silenced by violence to a global leader who has become a symbol for justice and equality, her story continues to inspire individuals everywhere to stand up for what they believe in.

eng-u2-rc1.title: Bài đọc hiểu Unit 2 (nâng cao) — Salad bowl, not melting pot
eng-u2-rc1.text: Sociologists once predicted that immigrants would melt into a single national culture, like ingredients dissolving in a stew. The reality in most diverse cities looks less like a melting pot and more like a salad bowl: each component retains its distinct flavour while contributing to the whole. Second-generation teenagers often embody this duality, switching effortlessly between the language of home and that of school. Such code-switching was once viewed as a handicap; recent research reframes it as cognitive flexibility. Festivals, cuisine, and music provide low-stakes arenas where cultures meet without coercion. Yet coexistence is not frictionless: competition for jobs and housing can harden group boundaries. Scholars argue that integration succeeds not when differences disappear, but when institutions guarantee equal dignity. In this view, multiculturalism is less a demographic fact than a daily negotiation.

eng-u2-cloze5.title: Bài đọc đục lỗ Unit 2 (nâng cao) — When cultures collide

(4) ____ years of immersion, most migrants achieve a stable bicultural identity. (5) ____ differences in values persist, daily friction diminishes. Host societies, for their part, must move beyond fear toward (6) ____ understanding.
